summary: Changes the recommended default for generating stable IPv6 interface identifiers with SLAAC to the method in RFC 7217, and recommends against embedding stable link-layer addresses. It updates several older RFCs.

eli5.summary: Your device used to build its network name from its hardware serial number, which let people track you. Now it builds a name that does not reveal that.

questions: what is a stable ipv6 interface identifier
why not use mac address in ipv6 address
subtitle: Why IPv6 devices should stop building their stable addresses from hardware addresses, and what to use instead.

tldr.problem: With SLAAC, hosts typically build the second half of a stable IPv6 address from a link-layer address such as a MAC address, which makes people and devices easy to track and scan.
tldr.mechanism: Nodes SHOULD use the method in RFC 7217 as the default way to generate stable addresses, and SHOULD NOT by default embed a stable link-layer address in the interface identifier.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track update to fourteen older RFCs that changes the recommended default; it leaves temporary addresses (RFC 4941) alone.

today: RFC 8064 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2464, RFC 2467, RFC 2470, RFC 2491, RFC 2492, RFC 2497, RFC 2590, RFC 3146, RFC 3572, RFC 4291, RFC 4338, RFC 4391, RFC 5072 and RFC 5121.

sections.title: The Problem With Link-Layer Based Identifiers
sections.content:
With Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), a host usually forms a stable address from a network prefix advertised by a local router and an Interface Identifier (IID). That IID typically embeds a stable link-layer address, such as an IEEE LAN MAC address.

The RFC points to RFC 7721 for the consequences: network-activity correlation, location tracking, address scanning and device-specific vulnerability exploitation. Reusing identifiers that carry their own meaning across different contexts can be harmful for security and privacy in general.

The RFC also notes that some popular IPv6 implementations had already moved away from the traditional scheme to reduce these problems.
sections.eli5: If your name at every school you visit contains your home phone number, anyone can recognise you everywhere. The old way of naming devices did something like that.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
Nodes SHOULD implement and use RFC 7217 as the default scheme for generating stable IPv6 addresses with SLAAC. By default, nodes SHOULD NOT use address generation schemes that embed a stable link-layer address in the IID.

The RFC names the schemes it recommends against for stable IIDs: those specified in RFC 2464, RFC 2467, RFC 2470, RFC 2491, RFC 2492, RFC 2497, RFC 2590, RFC 3146, RFC 3572, RFC 4338, RFC 4391, RFC 5072 and RFC 5121.

A link layer MAY define its own, more efficient mechanism for stable address generation that does not address the privacy concerns. In that case, whether to enable the privacy-preserving mechanism SHOULD be configurable.
sections.eli5: The rule is: by default, make your device's name from something that does not reveal its serial number. A network type with a good reason may do it differently, but then people should be able to switch the safer way on.

sections.title: What the Recommendation Covers
sections.content:
The recommendations apply only where an implementation would otherwise configure a stable IID containing a link-layer address. They do not change the existing recommendations on temporary addresses in RFC 4941, and they do not apply when SLAAC produces non-stable addresses, for example by embedding a link-layer address that is periodically randomized.

The document also adds no new requirements about when stable addresses are configured. A stable address here means one that does not vary over time within the same network.

The RFC accepts that stable addresses are often wanted: for network management, event logging, access control, quality of service, server or router interfaces, and long-lived TCP connections.
sections.eli5: This rule only changes how the permanent name is made. Short-lived throwaway names, and the choice of when to use a permanent name, are not touched.

sections.title: Why Some Networks Used Link-Layer IIDs
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges that in some network technologies, an IID based on a link-layer address has advantages. Its example is RFC 6282, which allows IPv6 datagrams over IEEE 802.15.4-based networks to be compressed when the IID is based on the underlying link-layer address.

Background on the traditional format is in RFC 4291, which defines the Modified EUI-64 format for IIDs and, in Appendix A, how to turn an EUI-64 identifier or a 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC address into one.
sections.eli5: Using the serial number as the name does have a benefit: some tiny low-power networks can send shorter messages that way. That is why the rule has room for exceptions.

sections.title: Future Work
sections.content:
The RFC lists documents whose mechanisms might need updating to be fully compatible: RFC 6282, RFC 4944 (IPv6 over IEEE 802.15.4), RFC 6775 (Neighbor Discovery optimization for 6LoWPANs) and RFC 7428 (IPv6 over ITU-T G.9959 networks).

Future revisions should consider the privacy and security issues and explain any design reasons for keeping stable IIDs based on a node's link-layer address.
sections.eli5: Some other rulebooks still use the old way. The authors ask whoever updates them next to think about privacy or explain why they cannot.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The whole document is a security and privacy measure. It recommends against the default use of predictable Interface Identifiers in IPv6 addresses, and recommends RFC 7217 as the default scheme for stable SLAAC addresses so that the issues of IIDs embedding stable link-layer addresses are mitigated.
sections.eli5: A name that cannot be guessed from your serial number is harder for strangers to follow or poke at.
